q-122846.name: Question 1
q-122846.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14247841/assets/ac4970f243e32138114e2f8973205d39e75ed95445a0b410e969e494672d2b37.png)

Consider the partition of the rectangular region $R$ shown above and the positive function $f(x,y)$ defined on $R.$ Which of the following gives an expression for the upper Riemann sum of $f$ with respect to this partition.

*Hint: ${M}_{ij}$ denotes the maximum value of $f$ on the subregion ${R}_{ij}$*
q-122846.worked_solution:
To calculate the upper Riemann sum $U$ with respect to the given partition, we compute the sum of the volumes of $3$ rectangular solids, one for each ${R}_{ij}.$

The volume of the rectangular solid corresponding to each subregion ${R}_{ij}$ is given by

$$
{M}_{ij}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{ij}).
$$

where ${M}_{ij}$ denotes the maximum value of $f$ on the subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ We pick the *maximum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *upper* sum.

So in our case, we have

$$
U={M}_{11}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{11})+{M}_{12}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{12})+{M}_{13}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{13}).
$$

Notice that

$$
\text{Area}({R}_{11})=\text{Area}({R}_{12})=\text{Area}({R}_{13})=2.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}U & =2\cdot {M}_{11}+2\cdot {M}_{12}+2\cdot {M}_{13} \\  & =2({M}_{11}+{M}_{12}+{M}_{13}).\end{aligned}
$$

q-123057.worked_solution:
To calculate the upper Riemann sum $U$ with respect to the given partition, we compute the sum of the volumes of $4$ rectangular solids, one for each ${R}_{ij}.$

The volume of the rectangular solid corresponding to each subregion ${R}_{ij}$ is given by

$$
{M}_{ij}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{ij}).
$$

where ${M}_{ij}$ denotes the maximum value of $f$ on the subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ We pick the *maximum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *upper* sum.

So in our case, we have

$$
U={M}_{11}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{11})+{M}_{21}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{21})+{M}_{12}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{12})+{M}_{22}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{22}).
$$

Notice that

$$
\text{Area}({R}_{11})=\text{Area}({R}_{21})=\text{Area}({R}_{12})=\text{Area}({R}_{22})=6.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}U & =6\cdot {M}_{11}+6\cdot {M}_{21}+6\cdot {M}_{12}+6\cdot {M}_{22} \\  & =6({M}_{11}+{M}_{21}+{M}_{12}+{M}_{22}).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Consider the partition of the rectangular region R shown above and the positive function f(x,y) defined on R. Which of the following gives an expression for the upper Riemann sum of f with respect to this partition.

Hint: Mij denotes the maximum value of f on the subregion Rij

a
6M11+M21+6M12+M22
b
6⋅M11⋅M21⋅M12⋅M22
c
6(M11+M21+M12+M22)
d
6M11+M21+M12+6M22
e
M11+M21+M12+M22
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To calculate the upper Riemann sum U with respect to the given partition, we compute the sum of the volumes of 4 rectangular solids, one for each Rij.

The volume of the rectangular solid corresponding to each subregion Rij is given by

Mij⋅Area(Rij).

where Mij denotes the maximum value of f on the subregion Rij. We pick the maximum value of f because we're finding the upper sum.

So in our case, we have

U=M11⋅Area(R11)+M21⋅Area(R21)+M12⋅Area(R12)+M22⋅Area(R22).

Notice that

Area(R11)=Area(R21)=Area(R12)=Area(R22)=6.

Therefore, we have

U=6⋅M11+6⋅M21+6⋅M12+6⋅M22=6(M11+M21+M12+M22).

Consider the partition of the rectangular region $R$ shown above and the positive function $f(x,y)$ defined on $R.$ Which of the following gives an expression for the upper Riemann sum of $f$ with respect to this partition.

*Hint: ${M}_{ij}$ denotes the maximum value of $f$ on the subregion ${R}_{ij}$*
q-123058.worked_solution:
To calculate the upper Riemann sum $U$ with respect to the given partition, we compute the sum of the volumes of $2$ rectangular solids, one for each ${R}_{ij}.$

The volume of the rectangular solid corresponding to each subregion ${R}_{ij}$ is given by

$$
{M}_{ij}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{ij}).
$$

where ${M}_{ij}$ denotes the maximum value of $f$ on the subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ We pick the *maximum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *upper* sum.

So in our case, we have

$$
U={M}_{11}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{11})+{M}_{12}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{12}).
$$

Notice that

$$
\text{Area}({R}_{11})=\text{Area}({R}_{12})=4.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}U & =4\cdot {M}_{11}+4\cdot {M}_{12} \\  & =4({M}_{11}+{M}_{12}).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4

Consider the partition of the rectangular region R shown above and the positive function f(x,y) defined on R. Which of the following gives an expression for the upper Riemann sum of f with respect to this partition.

Hint: Mij denotes the maximum value of f on the subregion Rij

a
5M11+3M21−M31
b
3(M11+M21+M31)
c
15M11+5M21+3M31
d
5(M11+M21+M31)
e
15(M11+M21+M31)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To calculate the upper Riemann sum U with respect to the given partition, we compute the sum of the volumes of 3 rectangular solids, one for each Rij.

The volume of the rectangular solid corresponding to each subregion Rij is given by

Mij⋅Area(Rij).

where Mij denotes the maximum value of f on the subregion Rij. We pick the maximum value of f because we're finding the upper sum.

So in our case, we have

U=M11⋅Area(R11)+M21⋅Area(R21)+M31⋅Area(R31).

Notice that

Area(R11)=Area(R21)=Area(R31)=15.

Therefore, we have

U=15⋅M11+15⋅M21+15⋅M31=15(M11+M21+M31).

Consider the partition of the rectangular region $R$ shown above and the positive function $f(x,y)$ defined on $R.$ Which of the following gives an expression for the upper Riemann sum of $f$ with respect to this partition.

*Hint: ${M}_{ij}$ denotes the maximum value of $f$ on the subregion ${R}_{ij}$*
q-123056.worked_solution:
To calculate the upper Riemann sum $U$ with respect to the given partition, we compute the sum of the volumes of $4$ rectangular solids, one for each ${R}_{ij}.$

The volume of the rectangular solid corresponding to each subregion ${R}_{ij}$ is given by

$$
{M}_{ij}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{ij}).
$$

where ${M}_{ij}$ denotes the maximum value of $f$ on the subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ We pick the *maximum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *upper* sum.

So in our case, we have

$$
U={M}_{11}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{11})+{M}_{21}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{21})+{M}_{31}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{31})+{M}_{41}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{41}).
$$

Notice that

$$
\text{Area}({R}_{11})=\text{Area}({R}_{21})=\text{Area}({R}_{31})=\text{Area}({R}_{41})=2.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}U & =2\cdot {M}_{11}+2\cdot {M}_{21}+2\cdot {M}_{31}+2\cdot {M}_{41} \\  & =2({M}_{11}+{M}_{21}+{M}_{31}+{M}_{41}).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Consider the partition of the rectangular region R shown above and the positive function f(x,y) defined on R. Which of the following gives an expression for the upper Riemann sum of f with respect to this partition.

Hint: Mij denotes the maximum value of f on the subregion Rij

a
2(M11+M21+M31+M41)
b
M11+M21+M31+M41
c
M11⋅M21⋅M31⋅M41
d
2M11+M21+M31+2M41
e
M11+2M21+2M31+M41
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

To calculate the upper Riemann sum U with respect to the given partition, we compute the sum of the volumes of 4 rectangular solids, one for each Rij.

The volume of the rectangular solid corresponding to each subregion Rij is given by

Mij⋅Area(Rij).

where Mij denotes the maximum value of f on the subregion Rij. We pick the maximum value of f because we're finding the upper sum.

So in our case, we have

U=M11⋅Area(R11)+M21⋅Area(R21)+M31⋅Area(R31)+M41⋅Area(R41).

Notice that

Area(R11)=Area(R21)=Area(R31)=Area(R41)=2.

Therefore, we have

U=2⋅M11+2⋅M21+2⋅M31+2⋅M41=2(M11+M21+M31+M41).

q-123231.name: Question 6
q-123231.problem:
Let $R=[1,4]\times [2,4]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)=16-xy.$
Further, let $P$ be a partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}=\{1,2,3,4\},\,{P}_{2}=\{2,4\},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the upper Riemann sum $U(f,P).$
q-123231.worked_solution:
First, let's draw the region $R$ and the partition $P.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14247841/assets/deff4f8b668e3c7327d92132f579c16d1f99dd5b52603b2f6afe6b7c6c5b7bb6.png)

The upper sum $U(f,P)$ is given by

$$
U(f,P)={M}_{11}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{11})+{M}_{21}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{21})+{M}_{31}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{31}),
$$

where ${M}_{ij}$ is the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ We pick the *maximum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *upper* sum.

Taking into account the fact that $\text{Area}({R}_{ij})=2$ for all $3$ subregions, the formula for $U(f,P)$ reduces to

$$
\begin{aligned}U(f,P) & =2\cdot {M}_{11}+2\cdot {M}_{21}+2\cdot {M}_{31} \\  & =2({M}_{11}+{M}_{21}+{M}_{31}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that

- $f(x,y)=16-xy$ decreases as $x$ increases, and

- $f(x,y)=16-xy$ decreases as $y$ increases.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14247841/assets/21cd2d1c002e5b66100396f9e4d5708b8ffd7fd2b9b6cc7b7078cd5507011a0d.png)

As a result, the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion is attained when we have the *smallest* possible $x$ and the *smallest* possible $y.$ This is the value at the *bottom left corner* of each subregion.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14247841/assets/9ebca45ee50cf0fe5f91e21427524600b26a512f10340c18c995c16f9cfe372d.png)

Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{11} & =f(1,2)=14 \\ {M}_{21} & =f(2,2)=12 \\ {M}_{31} & =f(3,2)=10\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}U(f,P) & =2(14+12+10) \\  & =72.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $R=[0,5]\times [1,5]$ be a region in the $xy$-plane, and let $f(x,y)=100-{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}.$
Further, let $P$ be a partition of $R,$ where

$$
\begin{aligned}{P}_{1}=\{0,5\},\,{P}_{2}=\{1,3,5\},\,P={P}_{1}\times {P}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the upper Riemann sum $U(f,P).$
q-123243.worked_solution:
First, let's draw the region $R$ and the partition $P.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14247841/assets/77fdf238fb2b4046da6ddc69024378a56e4de5f46de301d5fac094cbc290b23b.png)

The upper sum $U(f,P)$ is given by

$$
U(f,P)={M}_{11}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{11})+{M}_{12}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{12}),
$$

where ${M}_{ij}$ is the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ We pick the *maximum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *upper* sum.

Taking into account the fact that $\text{Area}({R}_{ij})=10$ for both subregions, the formula for $U(f,P)$ reduces to

$$
\begin{aligned}U(f,P) & =10\cdot {M}_{11}+10\cdot {M}_{12} \\  & =10({M}_{11}+{M}_{12}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that

- $f(x,y)=100-{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}$ decreases as $x$ increases, and

- $f(x,y)=100-{x}^{2}-3{y}^{2}$ decreases as $y$ increases.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14247841/assets/62871cd2fcc4993e0775fb7bdf0609d7849a1aa2ea5a314bc727967df590d6e7.png)

As a result, the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion is attained when we have the *smallest* possible $x$ and the *smallest* possible $y.$ This is the value at the *bottom left corner* of each subregion.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14247841/assets/9b814374a5b132560656d6fe2dc2350cb693847733a40c0d21b9a13be30025e1.png)

Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{11} & =f(0,1)=97 \\ {M}_{12} & =f(0,3)=73\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}U(f,P) & =10(97+73) \\  & =1\,700.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that

As a result, the maximum value of f in each subregion is attained when we have the largest possible x and the largest possible y. This is the value at the top right corner of each subregion.

$$

Calculate the upper Riemann sum $U(f,P).$
q-123133.worked_solution:
First, let's draw the region $R$ and the partition $P.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14247841/assets/0938d12d93c4f962a4ebd8daa7efe4543fc30c419be7d89f165e21bcadce84bb.png)

The upper sum $U(f,P)$ is given by

$$
U(f,P)={M}_{11}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{11})+{M}_{21}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{21})+{M}_{12}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{12})+{M}_{22}\cdot \text{Area}({R}_{22}),
$$

where ${M}_{ij}$ is the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion ${R}_{ij}.$ We pick the *maximum* value of $f$ because we're finding the *upper* sum.

Taking into account the fact that $\text{Area}({R}_{ij})=8$ for all $4$ subregions, the formula for $U(f,P)$ reduces to

$$
\begin{aligned}U(f,P) & =8\cdot {M}_{11}+8\cdot {M}_{21}+8\cdot {M}_{12}+8\cdot {M}_{22} \\  & =8({M}_{11}+{M}_{21}+{M}_{12}+{M}_{22}).\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that

- $f(x,y)=x+y$ increases as $x$ increases, and

- $f(x,y)=x+y$ increases as $y$ increases.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14247841/assets/af324138b21609cef59f49df0920ecc12681b8cb7667a843ff2d3fff3c27ea13.png)

As a result, the *maximum* value of $f$ in each subregion is attained when we have the *largest* possible $x$ and the *largest* possible $y.$ This is the value at the *top right corner* of each subregion. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14247841/assets/14b50472bce6d935803ca4f74bb5b1761903c0b0b015ce72e7e1e5e08f35868b.png)

Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{M}_{11} & =f(6,5)=11 \\ {M}_{21} & =f(10,5)=15 \\ {M}_{12} & =f(6,7)=13 \\ {M}_{22} & =f(10,7)=17\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\begin{aligned}U(f,P) & =8(11+15+13+17) \\  & =448.\end{aligned}
$$
